title: {{NAME}} and the Match That Saved the Nature Reserve
moral: Sometimes you fight for something not because you can win, but because it's worth fighting for.

pages.content:
The nature reserve was going to be turned into a shopping centre unless someone raised eighty thousand in thirty days.

The reserve's founder, old Mr Vance, had one idea: a charity football match. Heroes versus Legends. Celebrity names. Big crowd.

He needed someone to organise it.

The fox at the reserve entrance had been watching {{NAME}} for a week before Mr Vance found him. The fox had chosen, and Mr Vance trusted the fox's judgement implicitly.

"The fox picked you," Mr Vance said, by way of introduction.

"I'll do it," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
The organisation took three weeks.

{{NAME}}'s hero contacts came through: four professional heroes agreed to play. His football network delivered six former league players. The animals of the reserve were, he discovered, an extremely effective promotion team: every creature that could carry a flyer apparently did so.

The squirrels deposited flyers on every park bench in the city. The crows left them on doorsteps. The fox sat in the high street with a poster propped against it that he maintained {{NAME}} had arranged but that he had arranged himself.

"You're a natural marketer," {{NAME}} told the fox.

pages.content:
The match itself: two thousand people turned up, which was a thousand eight hundred more than anyone expected.

The heroes played with enormous enthusiasm and technically imperfect football. The legends played with skill and the light competitive glint of people who still hate losing.

{{NAME}} played too, in the reserve's team colours, and scored with a cross from the fox's position, which nobody understood except him.

The fox was not on the pitch. But it was watching from the reserve fence exactly where a winger would stand.

"I can see the angles from here," {{NAME}} explained later. Nobody believed him.

pages.content:
Final total: ninety-four thousand.

Mr Vance sat on the bench beside {{NAME}} as the crowd cleared, the number on a printout in his hand.

"Fourteen thousand over target," he said. "The reserve is safe."

The fox had entered the pitch at some point and was sitting on Mr Vance's other side with an air of someone who had expected this outcome all along.

"You trusted a fox's judgement," said {{NAME}}.

"The fox has better judgement than most people I know," said Mr Vance simply.

pages.content:
He walked through the reserve as it closed at dusk.

The animals had returned to their usual routines: the deer in the east meadow, the birds settling, the fox somewhere ahead of him on the path.

Every one of them was here because the reserve existed.

The reserve existed because of thirty days of effort and a charity match and a fox's recommendation.

He walked home in the last light, the reserve gate closing behind him.

In bed, he slept deeply, and in his sleep he could hear it: the reserve at night, alive and continuing.
